name: Common Cold
shortDescription: A mild viral infectious disease of the upper respiratory tract primarily caused by rhinoviruses.
generalInformation: Common cold symptoms typically peak within 2-3 days and resolve spontaneously within 7-10 days in immunocompetent individuals.
urgencyGuidance: Low – Routine home rest and symptom hydration.
overview: The common cold is an acute viral rhino-pharyngitis causing mild mucosal inflammation of nasal passages and pharynx.
plainEnglish: A simple head and throat infection caused by common viruses. It brings runny nose, light sneezing, and mild tiredness, resolving on its own in about a week.
clinical: Self-limiting acute viral upper respiratory tract infection (URTI) with transient mucosal congestion, minimal systemic inflammatory response, and no lower tract infiltrates.

name: Influenza
shortDescription: An acute viral respiratory illness caused by influenza viruses A and B characterized by sudden onset of high fever and myalgia.
generalInformation: Influenza presents with more abrupt onset and higher constitutional symptoms (fever, prostration) than the common cold.
urgencyGuidance: Moderate – Medical evaluation advised if high fever persists or breathing becomes labored.
overview: Influenza is a contagious respiratory infection that infects the epithelial cells of the respiratory tract.
treatments: Bed rest and plenty of fluids
Neuraminidase inhibitors within 48h if high risk (per doctor)
plainEnglish: The flu is a stronger viral infection than a cold. It hits quickly with high body heat, shivering, and deep muscle pains all over the body.
clinical: Orthomyxoviridae infection inducing rapid cytokine release, high febrile spikes, generalized myalgia, and risk of secondary bacterial tracheobronchitis or pneumonia.

name: Sinusitis
shortDescription: Inflammation or swelling of the paranasal sinus tissue lining, blocking mucus drainage.
generalInformation: Most acute cases start viral, but secondary bacterial colonization can occur if sinus ostia remain obstructed beyond 10 days.
urgencyGuidance: Moderate – Consult specialist if symptoms worsen after 10 days or orbital swelling occurs.
overview: Rhinosinusitis affects frontal, maxillary, ethmoidal, or sphenoidal paranasal air cavities.
treatments: Nasal corticosteroid sprays under medical advice
plainEnglish: Swelling in the small air pockets behind your cheekbones and forehead, causing a feeling of deep pressure, throbbing headache, and stuffed nose.
clinical: Edematous obstruction of osteomeatal complexes resulting in impaired mucociliary clearance, stagnant secretions, and facial tenderness over sinus cavities.

name: COVID-19
shortDescription: A contagious disease caused by the SARS-CoV-2 coronavirus with multiorgan tropism.
generalInformation: Presentation varies widely from asymptomatic to mild upper respiratory symptoms or severe acute respiratory distress syndrome.
urgencyGuidance: High – Monitor oxygen saturation (SpO2); seek emergency triage if SpO2 drops below 94% or breathing is labored.
overview: SARS-CoV-2 binds to ACE2 receptors, inducing pulmonary endothelial inflammation and hypercoagulability in moderate-to-severe courses.
treatments: Medical consultation for antiviral or corticosteroid protocols
plainEnglish: A respiratory virus that can feel like a severe cold or flu, but sometimes causes loss of taste and smell or difficulty breathing that requires oxygen monitoring.
clinical: SARS-CoV-2 mediated systemic infection with variable pulmonary alveolar damage, microvascular thrombosis risk, and post-acute sequelae (Long COVID).

name: Pneumonia
shortDescription: Infection that inflames air sacs in one or both lungs, which may fill with fluid or purulent material.
generalInformation: Pneumonia can be bacterial (e.g. Streptococcus pneumoniae), viral, or fungal. Requires urgent medical diagnostic confirmation.
urgencyGuidance: High – Requires urgent chest radiography and prompt physician consultation.
overview: Consolidation of alveolar spaces with inflammatory exudate, impairing physiological gas exchange.
treatments: Targeted antibiotics or antivirals determined by physician
prevention: Early treatment of lower respiratory infections
plainEnglish: A serious lung infection where the tiny breathing air sacs fill with fluid, causing sharp chest pain when breathing, persistent fever, and strong cough.
clinical: Lobar or bronchopneumonic consolidation with rales on auscultation, leukocytosis, and focal opacities visible on chest imaging.

name: Bronchial Asthma
shortDescription: A chronic inflammatory disorder of the airways characterized by episodic and reversible bronchospasm.
riskFactors: Allergen exposure (dust mites, pollen, pet dander)
generalInformation: Asthma triggers lead to airway hyperresponsiveness, smooth muscle contraction, and hypersecretion of thick mucus.
urgencyGuidance: Moderate to High – Acute exacerbation with silent chest or poor inhaler response is a medical emergency.
overview: Chronic bronchial hyperresponsiveness and reversible airflow limitation.
plainEnglish: A long-term condition where the breathing tubes become narrow and swollen, making a whistling sound and making it hard to catch your breath.
clinical: Reversible obstructive airway pathology mediated by IgE/mast cell activation, eosinophilic inflammation, and bronchial smooth muscle hypertrophy.

name: Hypertension
shortDescription: A long-term medical condition in which systemic arterial blood pressure is persistently elevated (≥ 140/90 mmHg).
generalInformation: Often termed the 'silent killer' because many individuals experience no noticeable symptoms until organ damage develops.
urgencyGuidance: Moderate – Routine clinical management; blood pressure > 180/120 with target organ symptoms is a hypertensive emergency.
overview: Persistent vascular resistance resulting in elevated cardiac afterload and microvascular shear stress.
treatments: Lifestyle modification (DASH diet, exercise, salt restriction)
plainEnglish: High blood pressure means the heart has to work harder than normal to pump blood through your arteries. Usually symptomless, but important to control.
clinical: Chronic hemodynamic strain promoting left ventricular hypertrophy, endothelial dysfunction, arteriolosclerosis, and accelerated atherogenesis.

name: Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus
shortDescription: A metabolic disorder characterized by hyperglycemia resulting from insulin resistance and progressive secretory defect.
generalInformation: Early stages may be asymptomatic; diagnosed by fasting plasma glucose ≥ 126 mg/dL or HbA1c ≥ 6.5%.
urgencyGuidance: Moderate – Regular physician follow-up; acute ketoacidosis or hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state demands emergency care.
overview: Progressive peripheral insulin insensitivity coupled with pancreatic beta-cell dysfunction.
treatments: Medical nutrition therapy and structured exercise
Oral hypoglycemic agents (e.g. Metformin, SGLT2 inhibitors)
Insulin therapy if beta cell reserve diminishes
prevention: Balanced diet rich in whole grains and fiber
At least 150 minutes weekly of aerobic exercise
plainEnglish: A condition where your body has trouble processing sugar from food properly, causing sugar levels in the blood to rise over time.
clinical: Chronic metabolic syndrome with peripheral insulin receptor downregulation, hepatic gluconeogenesis upregulation, and micro/macrovascular complication risks.

name: Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD)
shortDescription: A digestive disorder that occurs when acidic stomach juice travels back up into the food pipe (esophagus).
generalInformation: Persistent acid exposure can cause erosive esophagitis, strictures, or Barrett's esophagus over time.
urgencyGuidance: Low to Moderate – Differentiate carefully from cardiac ischemic chest pain.
overview: Incompetence of the lower esophageal sphincter (LES) allowing gastric contents to retrograde into the esophagus.
treatments: Proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) or H2 blockers under clinical guidance
Elevating head of bed during sleep
plainEnglish: When stomach acid splashes upward into the food pipe, causing a burning sensation behind your breastbone, sour burps, and throat irritation.
clinical: Retrograde flow of gastric acid past a hypotensive lower esophageal sphincter, producing epithelial mucosal injury and vagal-mediated reflex cough.

name: Migraine
shortDescription: A neurological disorder characterized by recurrent episodes of moderate to severe throbbing headache.
riskFactors: Specific sensory triggers (bright lights, loud sounds)
generalInformation: Often unilateral and pulsating, aggravated by routine physical activity, and commonly accompanied by photophobia and phonophobia.
urgencyGuidance: Moderate – Urgent consultation needed if headache is thunderclap (worst headache of life) or neurological deficits persist.
overview: Neurovascular headache syndrome involving the trigeminovascular pathway and cortical spreading depression.
treatments: Prophylactic pharmacotherapy for high frequency attacks
prevention: Maintaining regular sleep and meal schedules
Tracking and avoiding personal dietary triggers
plainEnglish: A severe, throbbing headache usually on one side of the head that makes you sensitive to light and sound, often making you feel sick to your stomach.
clinical: Trigeminovascular sensory activation releasing calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) and neurogenic inflammation leading to central sensitization.

name: Rheumatoid Arthritis
shortDescription: A systemic autoimmune inflammatory disorder causing symmetrical polyarthritis, primarily of small joints.
generalInformation: Typically presents with morning stiffness lasting > 1 hour, affecting metacarpophalangeal (MCP) and proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joints.
urgencyGuidance: Moderate – Early rheumatology referral within 6-12 weeks prevents irreversible bone erosions.
overview: Chronic immune-mediated synovitis leading to pannus formation and cartilage/bone destruction.
prevention: Early aggressive therapy to induce remission
plainEnglish: An autoimmune condition where your immune system mistakenly attacks the lining of your joints, causing stiffness, warmth, and swelling in fingers, wrists, and feet.
clinical: Autoimmune inflammation marked by rheumatoid factor (RF) and anti-CCP antibodies, synovial hyperplasia, and articular osteoclast activation.

name: Dengue Fever
shortDescription: A mosquito-borne tropical viral infection caused by the Dengue virus (DENV-1 through 4) transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes.
riskFactors: Living in or travelling to tropical and subtropical zones
Standing stagnant water near residential areas
Previous dengue infection (risk of severe secondary dengue)
generalInformation: Known colloquially as 'breakbone fever' due to severe retro-orbital headache and intense arthralgia/myalgia.
urgencyGuidance: High – Monitor platelet count and hematocrit closely; watch for warning signs like persistent vomiting or abdominal pain.
overview: Flavivirus transmitted by Aedes aegypti; potential progression to severe plasma leakage and dengue shock syndrome.
treatments: Strict oral and intravenous fluid maintenance
Paracetamol for antipyresis (avoid aspirin and NSAIDs due to bleeding risks)
plainEnglish: A tropical viral fever spread by daytime mosquito bites that causes sudden high temperatures, deep eye aches, severe joint pain, and skin spots.
clinical: Flaviviral endothelial tropism leading to thrombocytopenia, capillary permeability, plasma extravasation, and risk of hypovolemic shock in the critical phase.
